questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
Let $g(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(11-2x)$ and $h(x)=-6{x}^{3}.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =g(x)+h(x).\end{aligned}
$$

First, we differentiate $g(x).$ We express $g(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(11-2x)$ as the composite function

$$
g=\operatorname{cos}⁡u,\,u=11-2x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}u}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot (-2) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡u \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(11-2x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate $h(x)=-6{x}^{3}.$ 

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x}=-18{x}^{2}
$$

Hence,

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={g}^{′}(x)+{h}^{′}(x)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(11-2x)-18{x}^{2}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x+5)$ at the point where $x=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
The slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=2$ is given by ${f}^{′}(2).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,u=3x+5.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡u)\cdot 3 \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x+5).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=2,$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(2) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot 2+5) \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡11.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=2$ is $3\operatorname{cos}⁡11.$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
The slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{6}$ is given by ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,u=3x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡u)\cdot 3 \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{6},$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =3\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{6}$ is 

$$
m={f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6})=0.
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)$ at the point $(1+\pi ,-2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=1+\pi $ is given by ${f}^{′}(1+\pi ).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡u,\,u=x-1.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot 1 \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=1+\pi ,$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1+\pi ) & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(1+\pi -1) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $(1+\pi ,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-2) & =0(x-(1+\pi )) \\ y+2 & =0 \\ y & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Reciprocal Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
The slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is given by ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=\operatorname{cot}⁡u,\,u=2\pi -3x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=-{csc}^{2}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-{csc}^{2}⁡u\cdot (-3) \\  & =3{csc}^{2}⁡(2\pi -3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =3{csc}^{2}⁡(2\pi -\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =3{csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =3\cdot {1}^{2} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is $3.$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=\operatorname{csc}⁡u,\,u=5x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=-\operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\cdot (5) \\  & =-5\operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u \\  & =-5\operatorname{csc}⁡(5x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(5x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of the tangent line at the point where $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=-\pi /2} & =-5\operatorname{csc}⁡(5x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(5x){|}_{x=-\pi /2} \\  & =-5\operatorname{csc}⁡(5\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2}))\operatorname{cot}⁡(5\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =-5\operatorname{csc}⁡(-\frac{5\pi }{2})\operatorname{cot}⁡(-\frac{5\pi }{2}) \\  & =-5\cdot (-1)\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ is $0.$

$$

$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(-{csc}^{2}⁡u)\cdot (-3) \\  & =3{csc}^{2}⁡(2\pi -3x).\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Power of a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express

$$
f(x)=5(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{8}.
$$

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
f=5{u}^{8},\,u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=40{u}^{7},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =40{u}^{7}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =40(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{7}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-40{cos}^{7}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}$ if $y = 4\csc (5x + 3).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y = 4 \csc u, \qquad u = 5x+3.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = -4\csc u\cot u, \qquad\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 5.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-4\operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\cdot 5 \\  & =-20\operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u \\  & =-20\operatorname{csc}⁡(5x+3)\operatorname{cot}⁡(5x+3).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Composition of Trigonometric Functions Using the Chain Rule
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y = \tan u, \qquad u = \sin x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \sec^2 u,\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d x} = \cos x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡u\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$
